Capture files the Internet Archive cannot reach, and publish them as an archive.org item

Source: R/archive_capture.R
arccap.Rd

Downloads each URL from here, records its SHA-256, size and time in a manifest, timestamps the manifest with an RFC 3161 time-stamping authority, and, with archive.org keys, uploads the files, the manifest and its timestamp as one public archive.org item. The item is the mirror that fetchvrf falls back to, and the timestamp shows that these were the bytes on that date.

Usage

arccap(
  urls,
  dir,
  item = NULL,
  meta = list(),
  tsa = "https://freetsa.org/tsr",
  ak = NULL,
  sk = NULL,
  tmout = 600L
)

Arguments

urls

URLs to capture, or a wbsave result (its refused URLs are taken).

dir

A folder for the files and the manifest (created if needed).

item

Optional archive.org item identifier (5 to 100 letters, digits, dots, hyphens, underscores) to upload to; NULL (default) captures without uploading.

meta

Named metadata for a new item (title, creator, licenseurl, description, subject, ...); mediatype defaults to "data".

tsa

The time-stamping authority. "https://freetsa.org/tsr" is the default; NULL means no timestamp.

ak, sk

archive.org keys; default from the environment as wbsave reads them.

tmout

Seconds allowed for each download and each upload (default 600).

Value

A data frame of class rmbl_archive_capture, one row per URL: url, file, sha256, bytes, fetched_utc, status ("captured", "uploaded" or "failed: ...") and mirror (the archive.org download address, for fetchvrf); attributes manifest, timestamp (a tsvrf result, or NULL) and item.

Details

Some servers refuse the Internet Archive's crawler while serving everyone else: Save Page Now then reports that the target “cannot find” the page, or “blocks access” to it, although the page is there. Those URLs cannot be put in the Wayback Machine, but they can be captured by anyone who can reach them, and the capture can be published. Pass a wbsave result as urls to capture just the URLs it failed on with such a refusal.

The manifest (manifest.json) lists, for each URL, the file, its SHA-256, its size and the time it was fetched. The timestamp (manifest.tsr) is the authority's signed statement that the manifest's SHA-256 existed at its time; tsvrf checks it, as does openssl ts -verify. Each file's digest in the manifest ties the file to that time.

The upload uses the Internet Archive's S3-like API: each file is sent with a PUT, streamed from disk, to
https://s3.us.archive.org/<item>/<file>.
The first request creates the item with the metadata given. The keys are the same as for wbsave, so they are read from IA_S3_ACCESS_KEY and IA_S3_SECRET_KEY, or their _FILE twins. They travel only in the authorization header and are never written or printed. Publish only what the source's licence lets you redistribute.

References

Adams C, Cain P, Pinkas D, Zuccherato R (2001). Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Time-Stamp Protocol (TSP). RFC 3161. doi:10.17487/RFC3161

Internet Archive. ias3: the Internet Archive's S3-like API. archive.org/developers/ias3.html

See also

fetchvrf, wbsave, tsvrf.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # interactive()
w <- wbsave(urls)
lic <- "https://www.statcan.gc.ca/en/terms-conditions/open-licence"
meta <- list(title = "Statistics Canada tables (captures)",
             creator = "Statistics Canada", licenseurl = lic)
cap <- arccap(w, file.path(tempdir(), "capture"),
                       item = "my-statcan-tables-2026", meta = meta)
fetchvrf(cap$url[1], tempfile(), sha256 = cap$sha256[1],
               mirrors = cap$mirror[1])
}
